Duodenal atresia is the most common cause of high intestinal obstruction in neonates and classically presents with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium; it is frequently associated with Down syndrome and often shows a 'double bubble' sign on abdominal X-ray. Jejunoileal atresia is also common and presents similarly but may have more variable radiographic findings and greater distension. Meconium ileus—especially in cystic fibrosis—presents with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium; meconium is abnormally thick and inspissated, causing distal ileal obstruction. Total colonic Hirschsprung disease (a rare but severe variant) can present in the first days of life with functional obstruction, distension, and bilious vomiting due to proximal dilation and secondary dysmotility, though it is less commonly associated with true bilious emesis than mechanical obstructions—hence lower confidence. Other entities like annular pancreas or meconium plug syndrome are less likely given the acuity and severity, and NEC is unlikely without feeding history or systemic signs."}
